ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Emile Griffith Synthetic CCD

text.paragraph: Establishing care with his care partner for memory loss and confusion: cognitive testing, reversible causes, PTSD and depression screening with a safety assessment, falls, and the plan. Concerns: He wants to know why he forgets things and wants to keep living at home; He still dreams about the fight in which his opponent died and wants the nightmares to ease; His care partner worries about him getting lost and about managing as things change. [S]

tr.td: Sertraline 25 mg oral tablet, one tablet each morning
Sertraline 50 mg oral tablet, one tablet each morning

MRI of the brain without contrast, with susceptibility-weighted imaging: mild generalized atrophy, slightly more in the frontal lobes, with hippocampi in the normal range for age (medial temporal atrophy score 1 on each side); a small area of old injury (encephalomalacia with hemosiderin) at the tip of the right frontal lobe; seven microbleeds at the gray-white junction of both frontal lobes; a few small white matter hyperintensities (Fazekas 1); a cavum septi pellucidi; no infarct, mass, subdural collection or hydrocephalus

Neuropsychological testing, about three hours with breaks: slowed processing speed and reduced attention, set-shifting and verbal fluency; learning and free recall reduced but much better with cues and recognition (a retrieval pattern rather than rapid forgetting); naming, language and visual perception intact; consistent with mild cognitive impairment of frontal-subcortical type; effort measures valid; mood and PTSD symptoms noted as contributors

Cognitive processing therapy for PTSD with the clinic psychologist: twelve weekly sessions, adapted for memory problems (shorter sessions, written one-page summaries, phone reminders, and his care partner helping with practice between sessions, with his consent)
Advance care planning conversation, about 30 minutes, with him and his care partner; his capacity to name a health care agent and state his values was assessed and present
Physical therapy for balance and strength: ten sessions with a home exercise program (sit-to-stand, heel raises, tandem stance, walking program)

text.paragraph: Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

tr.td: Professional boxing from 1958 to 1977, 112 bouts over nineteen years: long exposure to repetitive head impacts; no source read records a count of knockouts or losses of consciousness
Title fight in 1962 after which his opponent died ten days later; lifelong nightmares and distress about it, in his own public words
Severe beating by a group of men in 1992, one with a baseball bat, with several months in hospital, much of it in intensive care; short-term memory problems reported since

list.item: Memory loss and confusion over about a year, worse in recent months, reported by him and his care partner: repeating stories and questions, losing the thread of conversations, mixing up days, two missed appointments, and once getting lost changing trains on a familiar route; cause to be found: resolved, confirmed [S]

Post-traumatic stress disorder, chronic, after two index events (a title fight decades ago after which his opponent died, and a severe assault thirteen years ago): nightmares, unwanted images, avoidance of fight footage, guilt and self-blame, being on guard in crowds, poor sleep; PCL-5 41: active, confirmed [S]

Mild cognitive impairment (mild neurocognitive disorder) with slowed processing, executive and memory-retrieval deficits, most likely due to traumatic brain injury from a nineteen-year professional boxing career and a severe assault; meets the NINDS research criteria for traumatic encephalopathy syndrome (a research diagnosis); Alzheimer's disease co-pathology not excluded: active, confirmed [S]

Personal history of traumatic brain injury: repetitive head impacts over 112 professional bouts, and a severe head injury in an assault thirteen years ago with months in hospital: active, confirmed [S]

tr.td: Establishing care with his care partner for memory loss and confusion: cognitive testing, reversible causes, PTSD and depression screening with a safety assessment, falls, and the plan
Two-week review, seen the same day by cognitive neurology: brain MRI, staging, traumatic encephalopathy syndrome and other causes, sertraline and sodium
Six-week review: neuropsychological testing, the diagnosis and the plan, PTSD treatment, safety and caregiver support
Four-month review: PTSD after cognitive processing therapy, mood, sodium, falls and caregiver strain
Six-month review: PTSD, mood, cognition, safety and the plan for the year ahead

Cognitive work-up under the Alzheimer's Association guideline: history from him and his care partner, MoCA, function, depression and PTSD screening, first-tier blood tests (blood count, metabolic panel, B12, TSH), a medicine review for anticholinergic and sedating drugs, a sleep apnea screen, hearing and vision checks, and brain MRI

Cognitive neurology consultation at the memory clinic to stage the impairment, weigh traumatic brain injury, traumatic encephalopathy syndrome, Alzheimer's disease, vascular disease and the effects of PTSD and depression, and choose further testing

PTSD treatment by shared decision: cognitive processing therapy with the clinic psychologist, weekly for about twelve sessions, adapted for memory problems; and sertraline 25 mg each morning, raised to 50 mg after four to six weeks if tolerated, with sodium checked two weeks after starting and after the increase; benzodiazepines avoided

Collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping steps, people to call, the clinic number and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; medicines kept by his care partner; PHQ-9 item 9 and safety reviewed at every visit
Falls: STEADI assessment, physical therapy for balance and strength with a home program, and a home safety check
Measurement-based care: PCL-5 and PHQ-9 at each chronic-care visit during treatment; MoCA yearly or sooner with change; medicine review every visit

After the diagnosis: no cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine, which are not shown to help mild cognitive impairment or traumatic brain injury; memory strategies (one calendar, phone reminders, a fixed daily routine), exercise, social activity, sleep and blood pressure care; repeat neuropsychological testing in twelve to eighteen months or sooner with change; Alzheimer's disease biomarker testing explained and declined for now, as it would not change his care
Travel and money safety: carry a card with his address and his care partner's number, share his phone location, travel with company on unfamiliar routes, and set up shared oversight of bills

Caregiver support: education about mild cognitive impairment and PTSD, the Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline (which serves all causes of cognitive impairment), a caregiver class and a burden check; the Medicare GUIDE model explained for if dementia develops later
Advance care planning while he can take part fully: a health care agent, his values and goals of care, at the annual wellness visit
Find the cause of the memory problems and explain it to him in a way he can take in
Mild cognitive impairment most likely due to traumatic brain injury; explained with his care partner present, at his request, with a written summary
A clinically meaningful fall in PTSD symptoms (PCL-5 down at least 10 points) by four months
PCL-5 from 41 to 26 after cognitive processing therapy and sertraline
Nightmares no more than about once a week, with at least six hours of sleep most nights
Nightmares about once every two weeks; sleeping about six and a half hours
No falls, with a balance and strength program
No falls; Timed Up and Go from 13 to 10 seconds after physical therapy and a home program

list.item: Independent in bathing, dressing, eating and walking; needs reminders for appointments and help with bills (Functional Activities Questionnaire 6, narrative); Timed Up and Go 13 seconds; one fall on ice last winter without injury; standing blood pressure 128/78 mmHg with no drop [S]

Alert, courteous and warm, with a ready laugh; tells stories in detail but loses the thread and repeats one; tearful when the title fight comes up; mood "down some days"; thought process logical; no hallucinations or delusions; denies thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone; insight good [S]
